atlas.description: Atlas Field is read at 6:40am in a truck cab with the windshield already full of daylight, or standing on a slab with the sun overhead — so the page is built like a jobsite drawing set: a flat, unlit, glare-proof ground of #EDEDE9, a neutral off-white with the faint grey of primed drywall and none of the cream that would make it look like stationery. On that ground everything is set in hard, un-tapered blocks. Type is the architecture: Oswald sets every headline at 600 and 700, condensed and vertical and stacked tight at 0.9 leading with slight negative tracking, so a three-word promise fills a band edge to edge like stenciled lettering on a site sign; where a headline needs to shout at scale it goes uppercase, where it needs to sound like a foreman it stays sentence case. Body copy is Barlow Semi Condensed at 400 and 600 — narrow enough to belong to the same family of forms, wide enough to read for a paragraph in bright light — set in short, blunt, left-ragged measures with no more than four lines per stack. Numerals, labels, spec tags and step markers run in Saira Condensed 500/700, uppercase and tracked wide, doing the work of a punch-list header or a material tag. The color world is three commitments and nothing else: deep charcoal #1C1C1A carries all body text, all rules, and entire inverted bands that drop in like poured concrete forms; a graphite blue-slate #3F4A52 handles secondary panels, schematic linework, and the quieter half of a two-tone diagram; and a single burnt coral-red #C33A1F is reserved absolutely for CTAs, active states, checkmarks in a completed row, and the one hairline that underlines the number in a stat — never for body text, never as a wash. Structure is brutalist and unapologetic: no rounded corners anywhere, no drop shadows, no gradients, no soft cards. Blocks are separated by 2px charcoal rules and full-width charcoal bands; content sits on a visible 12-column grid whose gutters occasionally show as thin slate lines; feature panels are plain rectangles divided by rules rather than floated boxes. Diagrams are sparse and schematic — a job route drawn as three connected squares and an arrow, a material count shown as a bar of filled and unfilled ticks, a day's schedule as a stacked timeline of charcoal bars with one coral block for the active job — all built from flat fills and 2px strokes, never illustrated or decorative, tool-like the way an isometric fastener diagram is tool-like. Photography sits inside these rectangles with hard square edges and no vignette: framed crews, phone-in-hand on a joist, dusty hands on a screen, a stack of lumber under an open sky. The rhythm is quick and decisive — dense stacks of short bands, punchy inverted interruptions, minimal breathing room — mirroring how a crew actually moves: load, drive, frame, close out, next.

atlas2.description: Atlas Field is read at 6:40am in a truck cab with the heater running, or standing on a slab in flat overcast light with a phone in one gloved hand — so the page is built as a deep-ink jobsite poster that stays legible under glare and never blows out a dark-adapted eye. The ground is a dense graphite ink #14181C, a near-black pulled off pure black so it reads like anodized tool housing rather than a void; body copy sits on it in a cool bone #E6E9EC at generous size, and the whole page behaves like a screen-printed safety poster: flat fields, hard edges, no gradients, no glow. Two accents do all the work and they come straight from the trade — a machine amber #F2A511 for hazard-tape emphasis, tally numerals, section labels and thin rules, and a slate-teal #3FBFBF for the calmer structural blocks, blueprint tint panels and secondary chips. Amber is the only color allowed on a CTA and it appears there as a solid block of pigment with ink-black text on it, the way a signal sign works. Panels are constructed as decisive rectangles of primary or secondary at full strength — a teal band the width of the page carrying benefit copy, an amber rule stack under a section title — so contrast, not decoration, carries the eye down the page. Typography is strictly geometric: headlines in Chivo at 900 and 700, set tight (-0.02em), all-caps for short kickers and sentence-case for long statements, its squared terminals and industrial proportions echoing stencil lettering on a site board without tipping into novelty; body in Hanken Grotesk 400 and 600, a humanist-leaning geometric that keeps long-form spec copy calm at small sizes; and Chivo Mono 500 in small letterspaced caps for the field-log furniture — job numbers, quantities, timestamps, feature labels like 04 / MATERIALS — the type of numeric evidence contractors trust. Spatial rhythm is poster-like and dense on purpose: information packed into clear rectangular zones, tight leading inside blocks, decisive gaps between them, hard 1px amber hairlines separating stacked facts. Imagery is treated as graphic blocks — square-cropped close-ups of the app in a working hand, a plywood-mounted material list, a phone showing a daily report against a partly framed wall, aerial-ish site plan sheets — always cropped so one operational thing dominates the frame, always butted flush against a color field so photograph and pigment share an edge. Language stays flat and true: no 'revolutionize', just 'Log today's materials in forty seconds'. The overall effect is confident, punchy, and unmistakably field-issued: a piece of equipment branding, not a SaaS brochure.

atlas3.description: Atlas Field is used with one hand, standing in a gravel lot at 7:40pm — the light bar on a skid steer still running, phone screen the brightest thing for fifty yards. So the page is built for that eye: a deep cool charcoal ground, #12181C, the color of wet asphalt after the crews have gone, with a slightly darker sibling #0C1114 for recessed bands and card wells and a lifted #1A2329 for panels that need to sit forward. Text is bone-cool #E4EBEE, never pure white — the tone of a laminated site drawing under a work lamp. The brand's steady voice is a jewel teal #1FA69A, the green-blue of a machine's LED strip and safety decal, used for icon strokes, section eyebrows, key numerals, active states, and thin 1px vertical rules that run down the left of feature blocks like light spilling from an open cab door. Supporting it is a cool slate blue-grey #8FA8B2 for secondary copy, dividers, table rules and quiet UI chrome. The one accent is a hi-vis amber #FFA524, borrowed straight from strobe beacons and equipment paint, and it is disciplined: buttons, focus rings, one underline on the sign-up link, nothing else — no amber body text, no amber washes. Contrast is the whole grammar here; the noir tradition means most of the page is dark and empty, and meaning arrives as a narrow edge of light. Type is humanist and cool-blooded: headings in Be Vietnam Pro at 600 and 700, a contemporary humanist sans with open apertures, slightly squared terminals and enough width in the caps to survive being read at arm's length in the dark; body in Cabin at 400 and 500, a humanist face with a faint mechanical squareness that reads like a well-kept equipment manual — plainspoken, generous x-height, no charm-seeking. A third voice, Roboto Mono at 400 and 500, handles only the hard facts: job codes, timestamps, material quantities, section labels in small tracked uppercase, the '14-day' in a stat — the language of a delivery ticket. Layout works on a strict 12-column grid with wide 96–120px gutters at desktop, but bands are deliberately uneven: a feature band pushes copy into columns 2–6 and lets the screen mockup run off the right edge into the dark; the next inverts and floats a narrow slate rule across the full measure. Screens of the app are shown as sharp-cornered rectangles with a hairline #8FA8B2 border and a soft teal glow bled beneath them, as if the phone were the only source of light on the page. Photography is deliberately sparse — four or five frames, each earning its place: a crew loading a trailer at dusk, hands on a phone against a rough framed wall, a truck bed with lumber and headlamps. Edges throughout are square; the concept's world is stud lines, level bubbles, cut lumber and printed forms, and nothing in it is rounded. The overall feel is quiet competence after hours: dark, roomy, unhurried, with one warm light always on.

hearth.description: This is a bakery seen at 7:10 in the morning, when a neighbor in a wool coat pulls out a phone on the sidewalk of Market Street to check whether the sourdough is out yet — bright coastal daylight bouncing off wet Portland brick, so the page must hold up in glare, not glow in the dark. The ground is a honeyed, sun-warmed wheat tone, #F2E3C6, closer to the crumb of a scored loaf or the raw wall of a proofing room than to paper: it is the site's actual color, not a neutral stage, and every band that isn't tinted or dark still carries that grain-lit warmth. Body copy sets in a deep pumpernickel brown-black, #2B1D14, which reads as ink soaked into flour sack rather than as pure black. The brand's structural color is a burnished crust ochre, #8F5A11, used for rules, small caps labels, the underlines of links, hours tables, and the honey-toned tint bands; supporting it is a deep hearth-brick #703326, a fired-clay red-brown for contrast bands where the type flips to wheat, for the process section's numbered stages, and for the dark inset panels behind visiting details. Interaction alone claims the one saturated note: a molasses-glazed amber #E08A2B, reserved strictly for buttons, focus rings, and hover states — never for body text or ornament. The letterforms hold the heritage tradition in a slab register: headlines in Zilla Slab at 600 and 700, whose squared, gently softened serifs and slightly narrow set feel like a hand-painted bakery transom or a nineteenth-century mill sack stencil, tracked a touch tight at large sizes so 'Bread Made Slowly' lands as one solid block of warm mass; body copy in Bitter at 400 and 600 with its true italic for asides and ingredient notes, a slab with enough humanist warmth to carry three-hundred-word paragraphs about fermentation without stiffness; and small-caps labels, prices, weights, and the hours grid set in Saira Condensed at 500 and 600, tracked wide in ochre — the compressed, unfussy voice of chalkboards, price cards, and receipt stubs. The spatial rhythm is stately and tactile: generous rules of hairline ochre separate thought from thought, section labels sit in a tight condensed line above each headline, and the page moves in unhurried, well-fed measures with substantial breathing room around imagery — but it is not a gallery; it is packed with the actual information a neighbor needs, so text sits close and legible in comfortable measures of roughly sixty-eight characters. A subtle paper tooth runs under everything, the faint fibrous surface of a flour bag, catching the honey ground so blocks feel printed rather than rendered. Cards for the daily selection sit as bled media above short text stacks — loaf name in slab, weight and price in condensed ochre, one honest line of description — with softly rounded corners echoing the rounded ear of a batard and the curve of a proofing basket. Imagery is the connective tissue: hands dusted white, a couche folded back, steam off a cooling rack, a wooden peel against brick, all soft-focus and gently lived-in rather than styled, never a hard product shot on white.

hearth2.description: This is a bakery page built like a botanical specimen catalog from a small New England agricultural press — flat, printed, and graphic rather than cinematic. The page ground is a real color, not a stage: a soft dried-sage green, #DCE3D2, the tint of a herbarium sheet that has sat in a barn window, and it holds every band on the page. Body text and headlines sit on it in a deep fermented-rye ink, #22271F, near-black but unmistakably green-shifted, so the whole page reads as two tones of the same plant. The brand tone is a mid pressed-sage, #4E5C3F, used for section labels, thin rules, specimen numerals and the tinted band that separates the process section; supporting warmth comes from an oat-flour cream, #F2EDDF, deploystrictly as inset panels, card grounds and the mat behind contained imagery — never as the page itself. The single accent is a fired brick-crust red, #A03A22, reserved for buttons, links and hover states only; it appears perhaps four times on the whole page and lands like a rubber stamp each time. Typography speaks pure grotesque, no serifs anywhere. Headlines are set in Saira Condensed at 700 and 600 — tall, narrow, tightly tracked, announcing 'DAILY SELECTION' and 'OUR PROCESS' in flat all-caps blocks the way a Swiss agricultural poster announces a harvest, with headline blocks kept to two or three lines and set solid so the letters stack into a graphic slab. Body copy is Hanken Grotesk at 400 and 500, a humanist grotesque with generous x-height and slightly open apertures that keeps the explanatory fermentation copy plain-spoken and friendly at 17–18px with roomy 1.65 leading. A third voice, IBM Plex Mono at 400 and 500, carries the archival machinery: small tracked uppercase eyebrows, specimen numbers, prices, weights and the hours table, so time and quantity always read as catalog data. Spatially the page is a dense catalog, not a luxury spread: bands stack close, each opened by a mono label and a hairline sage rule, item entries aligned to a hard left grid with prices flushed right on dotted mono leaders. Imagery is treated as pressed specimens — squared-off, flatly lit, botanical-edged crops of a cracked sourdough crust, a starter's bubbled surface, a split rhubarb stalk, wheat heads, a plum halved on parchment — each mounted on the cream mat with a hairline sage keyline, captioned in mono. Nothing glows, nothing blurs, nothing floats; the whole page has the honest tooth of uncoated stock and the composure of a printed record of one day's baking in Portland.

hearth3.description: Hearth & Crumb is set on a dark slate ground the color of a cold Portland morning before the shutters go up — #1C2226, a deep blue-grey with the temperature of wet granite and steel proofing racks, not black. Body copy and long text sit on it in a pale oat-bone #E4E2DA, which reads as flour dust on dark metal rather than white. The brand color is a cool jade #4F7A6A — the muted green of glazed mixing crocks and the painted trim on Old Port storefronts — used for section rules, subheads, tag chips, block borders and the flat fields that separate bands. A brass #B98B3C carries supporting weight: numerals, hours tables, prices, small caps labels, the hairline underscores beneath headings; it is the color of an oven door hinge and a loaf's crust edge, and it keeps the cool ground from going clinical. The accent is a hotter ember orange #D9541F, reserved strictly for calls to action, live availability states and hover — it is the only heat on the page, so it means something. The tradition is brutalist and it should be worn honestly: no soft cards floating on shadows, no gradients, no rounded gestures. Structure is declared, not decorated — thick 2–3px jade rules that run the full band width, hard-edged blocks butted directly against one another, flat color fields that change abruptly at the seam, text set flush left in strict columns with visible gutters, and 1px brass hairlines subdividing data (hours, loaf names, availability) like an oven schedule taped to a wall. Headlines are set in Oswald at 500 and 600 — a condensed grotesque with squared shoulders and tight sidebearings, architectural and precise, set in generous uppercase tracking for section labels ('DAILY SELECTION', 'OUR PROCESS') and in tight, almost-touching leading for the larger statements. Body text is Barlow Semi Condensed at 400 and 600, narrow enough to stay in the same typographic family as the headings but with open, humanist apertures so paragraphs about fermentation and starter feeding stay genuinely readable and warm. Numerals, prices, timings and the 12-hour fermentation figures are set in Saira Condensed 500/700 as an accent voice, tabular in feel and slightly mechanical, so the hours table and the bread list read like posted information rather than marketing. Spatial rhythm is dense and deliberate: sections press against each other with short, firm gaps, the type scale jumping hard between an 18px label and a 56px heading with nothing in between, and imagery arriving full-bleed at intervals to break the stack. Photography is moody and documentary — bread interiors torn open under raking light, the open mouth of the brick oven, a bench scraper on steel, flour on dark wood — always completely still, never styled or lifestyle-warm. Text over image is protected by planned solid slate panels or jade fields, never a lazy black wash. The overall feeling: a working bakery at 5 a.m., all steel and shadow and one hot door, with information posted plainly and nothing hidden.

lumen.description: Lumen Objects is browsed the way its lamps are seen: late, indoors, by a designer at a desk with the overheads off and a specification deadline tomorrow — so the page is a darkened room and the objects are the only light source in it. The ground is a cool Copenhagen slate, #191E26, a blue-grey with the temperature of harbour water at dusk; it never lifts to black and never warms to brown. Body copy sits on it in #DCE3E8, a cool bone with the softness of frosted glass so long paragraphs never glare. The studio's own color is emerald #3FA48C — used for rules, small caps labels, section markers, the thin keyline that runs under headings — pulled straight from the bottle-glass cullet the studio melts down. Sapphire #7FA6DC is the supporting note: the cold rim-light that appears on the shoulder of a blown vessel, used for hover states, quiet panel fills at 12% opacity, and the tint behind the Process steps. The single accent is a molten filament amber #E8A65A, reserved absolutely for CTAs and interactive focus — the color of hot glass at the end of the pipe, and the only warm thing on the page, which is exactly why the 'Request the trade catalogue' button reads as the one lit switch in a dark room. Type is humanist throughout: headings in Signika at 600 for section titles and 400 for standfirsts — a geometric-humanist face with soft, slightly flared terminals and open apertures that echo hand-formed glass rather than machined product; body in Karla at 400 with 500 for lead-ins, a grotesque with humanist warmth in its 'a', 'g' and 'e' that stays legible at 17px on a dark ground. Small labels — 'Collection 02', 'Trade', material notes, dimension specs — are set in Karla 500 at 11px, letterspaced 0.16em, uppercase, in emerald. Space is generous and still: bands breathe at 140–180px vertically, gallery items sit on wide gutters with long captions floated beneath in a narrow 34-character measure, and nothing is centered except where the copy is genuinely a statement. A hairline rule of #2A323D, one pixel, separates thoughts more often than a box does — the page is built from voids and light, not containers. Imagery is the whole argument: each lamp photographed against near-black falloff, glowing from within, the hand-spun striations and trapped bubbles of recycled glass raking across the surface where light passes through, tool marks and the pontil scar left visible. Cards are borderless — image, then a line of Signika, then a spec line — no frame, no shadow, no chrome, because a frame would be a second object competing with the lamp. Sharp corners everywhere: this is Danish, this is a cabinet, this is a plate in a catalogue raisonné. Motion is slow and cinematic, images settling into place like a shutter opening rather than bouncing. The overall feeling should be a cabinet of wonders after closing time — contemplative, expensive without shouting, and unmistakably about material rather than marketing.

lumen2.description: A darkened Copenhagen showroom after closing, where a handful of glass objects hold the only light: that is the entire page. The ground is a deep neutral charcoal #17181A — a graphite-grey with no warmth and no blue in it, the color of an unlit gallery wall — and it runs uninterrupted from the first pixel to the last, so that every photograph appears to be lit rather than placed. Body copy sits on it in warm cream #EFE7DA at a generous 1.65 line height, never pure white, so the text reads like paper catching lamplight. Two jewel accents do the work of colored gels: a deep bottle emerald #4E9C84 for section fields, rules and the quiet tinted panel behind the trade-catalogue enquiry, and a saturated night sapphire #8FAEDC for small type indicators, focus rings and the thin luminous underline that grows beneath links on hover. A single struck amber #C98A3F — the color of hot glass leaving the pipe — is reserved exclusively for calls to action: the catalogue request button, the enquiry submit, nothing else. Typography is strictly didone, Copenhagen's own gallery-catalogue register: headlines in Bodoni Moda at 400 for large editorial statements and 700 for the rare bold mark, set tall and tight (0.95 line height on display sizes, -0.01em tracking) so the hairline serifs and vertical stress read like engraved plate lettering; true italic Bodoni Moda carries pull-quotes from the glassblower. Body and interface text is Playfair Display at 400 and 500, its lower contrast and wider apertures keeping paragraph copy legible against dark ground where a true text didone would shimmer. Small labels — 'Copenhagen, DK', collection years, edition numbers — are set in Bodoni Moda 400 at 11px, letterspaced 0.22em, uppercase, in muted emerald. Spatially the page breathes like a museum: bands of 160–200px vertical air, a wide single measure of 62ch for narrative passages, and collection pieces presented as borderless plates — image, then a thin gap, then a cream name and a one-line material note, no boxes, no shadows, no card chrome. Corners are square everywhere, matching the cut edge of a glass plate and the crisp geometry of Danish gallery framing. Texture is a faint film overlay — the barely-perceptible grain of pushed night film — that unifies dark surfaces and stops the charcoal from going flat. Images are the only bright objects on the page and should feel laminated into the dark: glass rims glowing, molten interiors, a blower's forearm caught in furnace light, a Nørrebro workshop at dusk. The overall rhythm is slow and cinematic; nothing arrives at once, and each lamp resolves out of shadow as its own moment of discovery.

lumen3.description: Lumen Objects is staged on a cool slate ground — #22282E, the colour of a Copenhagen studio wall at four in the afternoon in November, a dense blue-grey that reads as stone rather than black and lets glass be the only bright thing on the page. Body copy and long-form reading sit in #E4E9EC, a cool bone-white with a faint blue cast, never pure white, so an hour of reading at a desk never glares. The brand's structural colour is #3E9F8F — a deep bottle emerald pulled straight from the studio's cullet bins, the green that recycled float glass turns when you look through its edge — used for rules, section labels, small-caps eyebrows, and thin architectural frames around the workshop imagery. Supporting it is #9DB4D4, a mineral sapphire that appears as a background field for the process band and as a shadowed counterweight, so the page moves slate → sapphire → slate like light passing through stacked panes. The single accent is #9BD3C1, a pale seafoam glow reserved exclusively for buttons, form focus rings, and link underlines on hover — the exact colour of light escaping the lip of a blown vessel — and it never touches body text or decorative fills. Typography is strictly geometric: headings in Space Grotesk at 500 and 700, its slightly cut, engineered terminals giving section titles a drafting-table precision that suits Danish modernism without any nostalgia, set tight (-0.02em) with generous leading; body in Hanken Grotesk at 300, 400 and 600, a humanist-tempered geometric with tall x-height that stays comfortable at 17–19px over long process descriptions; and a third voice, IBM Plex Mono at 400 and 500, uppercased and letterspaced +0.14em, carrying lamp names, dimensions in millimetres, edition numbers, glass batch codes and form-field labels — the vocabulary of a maker's spec sheet. Spatial rhythm is architectural and unhurried: a strict 12-column grid, wide 8–10rem band padding, and asymmetric splits where a single lamp photograph occupies seven columns against four columns of text separated by a full column of empty slate — negative space treated as a material, not leftover margin. Hairline rules of #3E9F8F at 1px mark thresholds between thoughts. Imagery is sharp and high-contrast throughout: single objects on seamless cool-grey sweeps, the glass rendered with hard specular highlights and deep transparent shadows, plus workshop frames of the gaffer's bench where molten glass glows against the dark. Cards drop their boxes entirely — image, then a mono caption, then a short paragraph, with whitespace as the only separator — and every corner in the system is square, matching the cut, faceted, planar logic of the objects themselves. The overall mood is stately and composed: a design-conscious buyer scrolling this at a studio desk should feel they are turning the pages of a well-printed Nordic product monograph rather than browsing a shop.

naturaleza.description: A tourist stands on a Defensa Street corner at ten at night, phone in hand, deciding where to eat — the page is read in the dark, lit by streetlamps and shop windows, so the site is built as a nocturnal ground rather than a lit page. The whole surface is a deep indigo-black, #0E1424, a blue-cast ink that reads like San Telmo cobblestone after rain, never neutral charcoal; every band sits on it or on a marginally lifted panel of #16203A so the page moves in tonal steps instead of stripes. Body copy is set in a cool bone-white #E6EBF2 at generous line height, and the two jewel accents come from the market stalls and the cathedral gilt: a deep-cut emerald #17A276 used as the brand color for panel edges, section labels, small underline rules and the thin keylines that box a dish name, and a warm brass gold #C9A24B as the supporting color for prices, numerals, the wordmark's leaf-mark and hairline dividers. Interaction alone carries a brighter emerald #1FC98C — reservation buttons, links on hover, the focus ring — and it appears nowhere else, so a single glowing button is always the brightest object on screen. Typography is strictly geometric: headings in Sora at 600 and 700, its confident circular bowls and flat terminals giving the restaurant name a modern, un-nostalgic authority that keeps the direction away from parrilla kitsch; body in Hanken Grotesk at 400 and 500, a humanist-leaning geometric that stays warm and legible at paragraph length; and for the menu itself, DM Mono at 400 and 500 in small tracked uppercase for dish categories, prices, hours and the address — the typographic voice of a chalkboard rewritten each morning. Spacing is airy and cinematic: wide outer margins, dish blocks separated by long vertical silences, and asymmetric splits that let a plated image breathe against emptiness rather than filling every column. Corners are square throughout, echoing the framed doorways, tiled thresholds and iron shutters of the neighborhood, and buttons are crisp rectangles with a one-pixel emerald edge. A faint film overlay lies over the whole page — a barely visible grain that keeps the deep indigo from going flat digital and ties the ground to the photography. Imagery is the direction's drama: single spotlit subjects — an empanada broken open on dark slate, chard-and-provoleta milanesa, a hand pouring mate, a shuttered antique-shop facade on Calle Defensa — each emerging from surrounding blackness with one hard raking light, so photographs and page ground fuse at their edges. Every image is contained and calm; nothing tilts, nothing scatters. The overall mood is still, confident and hospitable in a low-lit way: a candle-lit table in a 1900s townhouse, not a nightclub.

naturaleza2.description: Naturaleza Sabia lives on a deep ink-blue ground (#0F1A2B) — the color of a San Telmo doorway at dusk, of enamel signage on Defensa Street, of the Rio de la Plata after the market stalls fold up. This is a page read on a phone in a dim conventillo courtyard or on a hotel bed after a long day of cobblestones, so the screen glows rather than glares: cool, low, jewel-lit. Body copy sits in a soft bone white (#EDE7DA) that never bleaches to pure white, and the whole page is built on art-deco discipline — strict vertical stems, stepped ziggurat margins, thin gold hairlines that bracket headings the way brass inlay brackets a Confitería mirror. The brand's own green is a jade-lacquer #4FA98F used for flat fields, section grounds and the shoulders of pull-quotes; the supporting metallic is a brushed champagne gold #C8A44D that draws every rule, frame corner and small-caps label. The single accent, reserved strictly for buttons, links and hover states, is a hot Malbec-tinged carmine #D6414E — the one moment of heat, borrowed from a chimichurri jar and a tango poster, never used for running text or ornament. Typography is entirely geometric: headings in Poppins at 600 and 700, set tight and generously letter-spaced in uppercase for section titles, its perfect-circle bowls echoing the compass-drawn geometry of 1930s Buenos Aires facades; body in Questrial 400, an open geometric single-weight face that keeps long English descriptions calm and unfussy for readers whose first language may not be English; and an accent face, Josefin Sans at 300 and 600, in wide-tracked small caps for dish names, prices, hours and the numerals on the map card — a deliberately deco silhouette with its high waist and small x-height. Dynamic diagonal tension runs through the layout: section titles and gold rules tilt on a shallow angle, image edges are cut on a consistent diagonal shear, and columns start at unequal heights so the eye zigzags down the page instead of marching. Ornament is sparse and structural — stepped gold corner brackets on menu groups, a doubled hairline (thick over thin) under every section title, chevron dividers that recall the parquet of an old San Telmo floor. Photography is the jewel: empanadas de humita, provoleta of grilled king oyster mushroom, blistered squash, purple radicchio, deep red chimichurri — saturated produce blazing out of the dark ground, framed by thin gold keylines. Cards are dense and confident, generous internal padding but tight vertical rhythm, so the menu reads like a well-set bill of fare rather than a brochure. Overall mood: nocturnal, opulent, a little rebellious, unmistakably porteño — the warmth comes from the food and the gold, not from beige.

naturaleza3.description: A tourist opens this page on a phone at midday, standing on the cobblestones of Defensa street with the sun bouncing off pastel facades, or plans dinner from a sunlit hostel courtyard — so the page is bright, printed, and legible in glare, never a candlelit dark room. The ground is a pale ash-grey newsprint neutral, #EDEDE8, the colour of a 1950s Buenos Aires broadside before ink; body copy sits on it in a deep bitter cacao-black #22201C for full daylight contrast. Over that stone-pale canvas the direction runs two poster inks: a warm crimson #B5203A borrowed from feria awnings and vermouth labels, and a golden-amber #8A5209 pulled from dulce de leche and toasted provoleta. Crimson does the heavy lifting — full-bleed poster bands, oversized dish numerals, botanical linework; amber underlines, rules, and the graphic burst behind a dish name. A single loud interaction green, #2E6B3E (the green of chard, chimichurri, and San Telmo shutters), is reserved strictly for reservation buttons and links so it reads as the one clickable colour on the page. Typography speaks in display serif throughout: headlines in Bodoni Moda at 700 and 900, its razor hairlines and vertical stress giving the swaggering, ink-heavy authority of mid-century Argentine advertising set large and tight, with numerals and dish names allowed to run to poster scale; body copy in Petrona at 400 and 600 with its true italic for captions and Spanish dish names — a warm, slightly rustic text serif that keeps long descriptions of empanadas and locro friendly rather than austere. Flavour notes, prices, and the small tracked labels ('Plato Fuerte', 'Since 1954-style poster caption') come from Cormorant Infant 600 in small caps-like uppercase, giving a printed menu-card voice. Spatially the page behaves like a folded broadsheet: dense stacks of type against sudden crimson colour fields, dish blocks set in unequal columns so the eye zigzags, generous ink-free gutters around each poster band, and hand-drawn botanical illustrations — zapallo vines, laurel sprigs, sunflower heads, thistle — drawn in single-weight crimson line and allowed to run off the edge of a band or tuck behind a photograph's corner. Paper tooth sits under everything so flat crimson reads as printed ink rather than screen fill. Rules are hairline-thin amber; corners are square everywhere, because this whole world is a printed sheet cut with a guillotine. The mood: appetite, confidence, sunlight, a menu you'd pin to a wall.

portfolio.description: A stark interrogation-room ground of #101012 — a true neutral graphite-black with no warmth and no blue drift — carries the entire page, so that every photograph reads as a lit rectangle floating in darkness the way a projected slide reads in a blacked-out newsroom. Text is set in #F2F2F0, a bone-white with the faintest paper cast, and it is the only bright thing on the page besides the images themselves. Two supporting greys do the structural work: #96979B, a cold ash used for captions, dates, place-names and hairlines, and #A8A9AC, a lifted charcoal used for the rare divider band or the pressed state of a link, never as a decorative fill. The single accent is #C8342B — a flat, unglossy oxblood-signal red pulled from Argentine political poster stock and the ink of a wire-service stamp; it appears only on interactive things (the inquiry button, a focus ring, an underline that draws on hover) and never in body copy or ornament. Typography speaks pure grotesque. Headlines and section markers are Space Grotesk at 500 and 700, its slightly mechanical, squared terminals and tight apertures giving captions the clipped authority of a picture-desk slug rather than the polish of a gallery label; set large, tightly tracked at -0.02em, in short lines that stop early and let black space take over. Body and caption copy is Archivo Narrow at 400 and 600 — a condensed news grotesque descended from wood-type headline stock, economical enough that a two-line historical context note under a photograph sits as a dense, factual block without ever competing with the image above it; small caps-style labels (year ranges, city, series titles) run at 11–12px, uppercase, letterspaced 0.14em in ash grey. Spatially the page is theatrical and airy: enormous vertical intervals between bands, images allowed to run edge-to-edge or sit as single lit plates with wide black margins, and long stretches where a single sentence of positioning statement holds a whole screen alone. Bodies of work are presented without card chrome at all — photograph, then a hairline of silence, then a small uppercase series label, then two lines of context — whitespace and darkness are the only separators, so the gallery reads as a sequence of frames rather than a grid of products. Corners are square everywhere, edges are hard, no shadow, no glow, no bevel: this is a world of contact sheets, tape marks, and light falling off into nothing. A very fine film tooth sits over the ground so the black never looks like a flat screen fill, and motion is slow, directional and cinematic — long masks pulling images out of black, focus settling — so that scrolling feels like a projectionist advancing through a reel rather than a website animating.

portfolio2.description: This is a portfolio built for the way it is actually used: a picture editor in Buenos Aires or Madrid opening a link late at night, screen bright in a dim room, scrolling slowly through twenty years of Argentine streets — so the page is a darkroom, not a gallery wall. The ground is a cool, slate-tinged near-black, #12161A, the color of a fixer tray under a safelight rather than a pure digital black; secondary surfaces and section shifts step up to #1B2126, a bluish charcoal that lets one band separate from the next without a single visible border. Body copy sits on that ground in #E4E8EA, a cool platinum-paper white with the faint blue of a selenium-toned print, while headings and lead lines take #F5F7F8 — the paper base itself, the brightest value in the direction and reserved for type and image highlights alone. A muted steel blue, #6E8494, carries captions, dates, place names and the thin metadata rules: it reads as pencil on the back of a print, quiet enough never to compete with a photograph. The one interactive color is #D8543B, a bleached darkroom-red used only for links on hover, the contact button and the focus ring — never for a heading, never as a fill, never decorative; it appears roughly three times on the whole page and each time it means 'act'. Type is strictly geometric: Poppins at 500 and 600 for headings, set with tight tracking and generous leading so the name and the thematic section titles read as clean, unsentimental labels — the lettering of a press credential rather than a magazine masthead. Body and standfirst copy use Work Sans at 300 and 400, its open geometric skeleton keeping long English paragraphs about protests, crises and elections legible at length without any editorial warmth. Metadata — years, frame numbers, locations, the '2001 / 2026' spans that head each thematic run — is set in IBM Plex Mono 400, uppercase, letter-spaced wide and sized small in #6E8494, like the strip of information handwritten along a contact sheet. Space does the rest of the work: enormous vertical air between bands, images given whole regions of shadow to sit in, text measures held narrow (about 58 characters) and pushed to one side so the eye always returns to the picture. Photographs are never boxed, never rounded, never given a shadow or a caption plate; they land as flat rectangles of light against the charcoal, media above a plain text stack with whitespace as the only separator, and a thin #6E8494 hairline occasionally marking a chronological threshold. A fine film-grain overlay unifies the ground with the imagery so screen and print share one tooth. The overall temperature is cold, still and forensic — high-contrast platinum tones suspended in shadow, absolutely no gradients, no glow, no ornament beyond the rule and the mono numerals.

portfolio3.description: A photo desk at 2am: an editor in Buenos Aires or Berlin scrolling this page on a dimmed screen, the room dark, the pictures the only light source — so the page itself is night. The ground is a cold charcoal, #16191D, a slate-blue-shifted black that reads as developer-tray dark rather than pure ink, and it holds every band from top to bottom; text on it is #F2F4F6, a faintly cool white with the same bluish cast as a fixer-washed print. Between them lives #8C97A3, a wet-pavement slate used for captions, dates, place names, event years and hairline dividers, and #8C97A3, a deeper gunmetal used for the thin 1px keylines, quiet card edges and the seam between sections. One color earns its keep as interaction alone: #C7452E, an oxidized flare red pulled from Argentine political ephemera — pintada spray on a Plaza de Mayo wall, the red of a stencilled banner in a night crowd — reserved strictly for link underlines on hover, the contact button and the focus ring, never for body text or fills. Nothing else is colored; the photographs carry all remaining tone. Typography speaks pure didone. Headlines and the photographer's name are set in Prata — a single-weight modern with knife-thin hairlines, ball terminals and severe vertical stress that at large sizes goes from elegance to a kind of forensic sharpness against dark ground; it appears at very large display sizes and again small for section titles, never in bulk. Body copy, captions and the about paragraph are set in Gelasio at 400 and 600 with true italic, a transitional-to-modern text face with enough sturdiness to hold at 15–16px on charcoal, its italic used for image locations and years. A third voice, Archivo Narrow at 500, handles the small tracked machinery of the page — 'BUENOS AIRES', 'ARCHIVE 2005–2025', frame numbers, contact labels — in 11px uppercase with 0.16em tracking and slate color, evoking a wire-service slug line. Spatial rhythm is gallery-slow and image-led: images arrive one after another at generous scale with wide charcoal margins around them, long vertical silences between bands (120–180px on desktop), and caption blocks tucked beneath left edges at half the image width so the eye returns to the picture. No cards, no boxes, no shadows, no rounded corners — media sits flush against the dark with hairline #8C97A3 rules the only ornament, occasionally a single rule spanning the measure to mark the shift from portfolio to about. The mood is unblinking, patient, cold-blooded but not cynical: darkness as a viewing condition rather than a style, tension held in the space between frames. A faint film-grain tooth lies over the whole page, just enough to keep the charcoal from looking like flat digital black.

pulso.description: Neon Nights Stockholm lives on a warm, sun-bleached ground — a pale peach-tinted white (#FBF1E9) that reads like the matte card stock of a 1985 synth-pop sleeve left in a window, not like paper and not like screen black. Against it, three pastel bands do all the structural work: a saturated peach-coral (#C2452A) as the primary voice, a cold mint (#1E6E5E) as its counter, and a soft electric lilac (#B79CF2) holding the middle. Body copy and rules are a deep graphite-violet (#221B33) that keeps the whole thing crisp rather than sugary, and a hot magenta (#C40068) is reserved strictly for CTAs, ticket buttons, and interaction states — never for text blocks or decoration. Color arrives as flat geometric fields, hard-edged bands, and stepped rectangles that stack in register like a CMYK misprint, with occasional 1px mint/coral channel offsets on headline edges to suggest RGB separation; there are no soft blurs and no unmotivated gradients — the only gradient permitted is a two-stop peach-to-lilac wash inside a bounded band, always terminating on a hard edge. Typography locks the grid: headings in Saira Condensed at 700 and 800, wide-shouldered and tightly set in all caps with slightly negative tracking so words read as machine-cut slabs; body in Barlow Semi Condensed at 400 and 600, narrow enough to keep long schedule copy dense and modern, open enough to stay legible on a phone in a dark queue; and Share Tech Mono at 400 for time codes, set numbers, stage labels, ticket tiers, and the small bracketed system-status tags ([DOORS 21:00], [WORKSHOP 14:00]) that thread through the page like readouts from an old terminal. Everything sits on a strict 12-column modernist grid with visible alignment: sections are separated by full-width color bands rather than whitespace alone, labels align to the same left rail down the entire page, and the numeric — set times, night one / night two, ticket prices — is always oversized and monospaced. Texture is minimal and clinical: fine 1px graphite hairlines subdividing bands, a faint horizontal scanline tint only inside dark color fields, and small stepped-corner notches where two bands meet. Motion is staccato — quick, snapped arrivals, tiny 60–120ms channel-shift flickers on hover, nothing that floats or eases lazily. The overall mood: a precise, bright, warm municipal control panel for a night of very loud music.

pulso2.description: Neon Nights lives on a warm, sun-bleached ground the color of a faded arcade flyer left in a Stockholm window — #FBF1E6 — a cream that reads as printed paper warmed by a CRT rather than as neutral white, and every band of the page sits on it or on one of two melting gradient fields drawn from it. The color world is airbrushed 1984-imagining-2084: mint #186B5E and lavender #6B45C4 are the two structural hues, laid as slow vertical washes that fade into the cream at their edges the way retouched Japanese city-pop sleeves fade, with blush #F7A8C4 pooling where they meet. Text is set in a deep aubergine-ink #2B1E3F rather than black, so headlines glow rather than punch; hot magenta #D6006A is reserved strictly for tickets, buttons, links and hover states, where it carries a single soft outer bloom like a neon tube behind frosted glass. Typography is fully geometric: headlines in Chillax — no, in **Poppins** at 600 and 700 with generous negative tracking on large sizes, its perfect-circle bowls and single-storey feel supplying the retro-futurist chrome-lettering silhouette without novelty, and secondary display lines set in wide letter-spaced uppercase; body copy in **Hanken Grotesk** 400/500, a humanist-leaning geometric with open apertures that stays calm and legible in long workshop descriptions and set-time lists; numerals, set times, stage labels and DJ credits are set in **Space Mono** 400/700, uppercase and tracked, which anchors the schedule tables and gives the page its telemetry, arcade-readout register. Spatial rhythm is generous and cinematic: very wide outer margins, headlines allowed to run large and lonely, then dense monospaced schedule grids that suddenly compress the eye — festival poster logic. Ornament is kept to a strict retro-futurist vocabulary: single hairline gradient rules, thin chrome-edged pill buttons, and soft radial glows behind imagery, never grids of wireframe triangles or clip-art palm trees. Imagery floats in layered depth — subject on one plane, a haze plane in front of it, a gradient plane behind — with everything rounded, soft-shouldered, and slightly out of the era it claims. The overall mood is a 3am Stockholm gallery in June, when the sky is still lavender and the sound system is still on.

pulso3.description: Neon Nocturne lives on a deep charcoal-slate ground (#12141C) — the cool, blue-shifted dark of a Stockholm warehouse gallery at 2am, lit only by projector spill and the exit signs. Body copy sits on it in a soft pastel ice (#DCE4F2), never pure white, so text reads like it's already been through a CRT. Against that void, three signals: electric cyan (#3BF0E4) as the primary, carrying section labels, hairline dividers, glyph clusters and the thin scanline rules that separate bands; a saturated magenta (#FF4FD8) as the secondary, used for the chromatic-aberration offset behind headlines (a 2px magenta ghost to the left, cyan ghost to the right, a printing-press misregistration frozen at the moment of glitch); and acid lime (#C6FF4A) reserved strictly for CTAs and interactive states — the ticket buttons, the hover on a DJ name, the focus ring — so lime always means 'this does something'. Nothing decorative wears lime. Typography is uncompromisingly geometric, the language of Swedish transit signage crossed with 1980s Japanese synth sleeves: Chakra Petch at 700 for display headlines — a squared, slightly clipped geometric with beveled terminals that already looks like it's rendering on a low-res display — tracked wide and set in uppercase for the festival name and section titles, and Space Grotesk at 300/400/500 for body, standfirsts, schedule rows and small print, its quirky geometric humanism keeping long paragraphs readable rather than robotic. A third voice, Major Mono Display, handles set times, dates, ticket tiers and stage numbers — monospaced numerals that echo timecode burn-in and cue-sheet printouts, always in cyan or pastel ice at small size with generous letterspacing. Spatially the page is dense and quick: tight vertical rhythm, band after band arriving with different backgrounds — the charcoal void, then a full-bleed magenta-to-cyan gradient field with charcoal text punched out of it, then the void again — so scrolling feels like moving between rooms of an installation rather than reading a document. Lineup rows are set as a hard grid of hairline cyan rules with names in Chakra Petch and times in mono, split into NIGHT 01 / NIGHT 02 columns. Installation and workshop cards bleed their imagery to the edge with only a padded text block beneath, corners hard-square everywhere — no softness, this world is made of pixels and cut vinyl. Texture comes from a fine film-grain veil over the whole page plus horizontal scanline banding at 6% opacity across image bands, with occasional RGB channel-split on hover. Surreal ornament appears sparingly and specifically: wireframe grid horizons, a lone chrome sphere, palm silhouettes rendered as cyan vector outlines rather than photographs — one per band at most, always geometric, never a stock vaporwave collage. The overall feeling: exclusive, cold, electric, a little corrupted — a festival poster transmitted from a satellite that's losing signal.

tbilisi.description: The page reads like a hand-bound Georgian manuscript left open on a wine-stained oak table in a stone cellar off Sioni Street. The ground is a deep charcoal-brown #1E1714 — the color of a soot-darkened marani wall — with body copy set in a warm parchment #EDE0CC that never glares. Terracotta #A6432A carries the brand: the fired clay of the qvevri buried under the courtyard, used for rules, small caps labels, section numerals and the underlines of links. A muted olive-bronze #6E6A45 — the color of dried tarragon, walnut skin and old brass — supports as a second surface tint for alternating bands and quiet borders. Aged gold #C79A3E is reserved strictly for calls to action and interactive states: the reserve button, hovered links, the phone number pill; it never appears as body text or wallpaper. Typography is the direction's spine. Headings are set in Cormorant Garamond at 300 and 600, its high-contrast, slightly nervous strokes echoing the engraved Mkhedruli letterforms and the copperplate title pages of 19th-century Tbilisi print shops; display sizes run generously large with tight leading and a whisper of positive letter-spacing on small-caps eyebrows. Body text is Spectral at 400, 500 and 600 with true italics for dish transliterations (khinkali, chakapuli, badrijani nigvzit) — a sturdy serif with open counters that stays warm and legible on the dark ground. Spatial rhythm is slow and reverent: tall vertical padding between bands, wide outer gutters, long single-column measures of 62–68 characters, and generous negative space around each photograph so it can be looked at rather than scanned. Texture comes from restraint plus craft: a barely-there film-grain overlay across the whole page, hairline terracotta rules that terminate short of the column edge, and an ornamental motif drawn from Georgian carved wood — a repeating grapevine-and-tendril fret used only as a thin 1px-height divider between major sections and as a small emblem beneath the restaurant name. Buttons are square-cornered, outlined in aged gold with a 1px stroke, filling solid gold with charcoal text on hover, no shadows anywhere. Menu items sit as borderless stacks: photograph, then a Cormorant dish name, then a Spectral description, separated by whitespace and a short terracotta rule rather than a box. Nothing bounces, nothing glows — the entire surface behaves like candlelight on clay: warm, matte, slightly uneven, and utterly still until you approach it.

tbilisi2.description: This is a page built like a wall of Old Town limestone: dry, warm, and quietly monumental. The canvas is a cool bone-cream (#F2EDE4) that reads like lime-washed plaster under overcast Tbilisi light, with a slightly deeper stone tone (#DCD3C4) used for alternating bands, table-of-dish rules, and inset panels so sections stack like courses of masonry. Body text is a near-black charcoal (#22201D) — the color of soot on a tone oven — never pure black, always with a trace of brown in it. The brand voice color is a deep oxblood wine (#6B2231), drawn from qvevri-aged Saperavi: it carries section eyebrows, small caps labels, drop-rule accents, and the thin hairlines that separate menu items. A supporting warm walnut (#8A6A4B) handles secondary text, captions, hours tables and the muted borders around photographs, echoing the aged wood of tavern benches. A single burnished brass-gold (#C08A2E) is reserved exclusively for interaction — the reserve button, phone link, directions link, hover underlines — and appears nowhere else, so a spot of metal always means 'act here.' Typography pairs a high-contrast display serif with an unfussy grotesque: headings in Playfair Display at 500 and 700, with true italics used for Georgian dish names and pull-quotes so the page carries an echo of calligraphic script and the curling ornament of a Mkhedruli hand; body, labels and navigation in Karla at 400, 500 and 700, set slightly wide with generous line-height and using its uppercase small-label register (letterspaced ~0.14em) for section markers like MENU, HERITAGE, HOURS. The rhythm is slow and reverent: very generous vertical air between bands (nothing crowds), a wide measure of no more than 62 characters, and menu entries laid out as an old chalked ledger — dish name in italic serif on the left, leader hairline in walnut, price in tabular Karla on the right. Texture is essential: a faint uneven paper/limestone grain sits over the cream background at very low opacity, edges of panels are drawn with 1px walnut rules rather than shadows, and photographs are given a thin cream mat and a hairline charcoal keyline so they read as prints hung on plaster rather than web tiles. Ornament is restrained and cultural, not decorative kitsch: a single repeated grapevine/qvevri-derived hairline motif in oxblood used as a section divider, at most twice per screen. Imagery is documentary in spirit — steam off a khinkali plate, hands tearing shoti bread, a narrow cobbled Old Town lane with wrought-iron balconies, an empty tavern interior before service — always observed, never staged. Nothing bounces, nothing glows; the whole page should feel like it was set in metal type, printed on stone-colored stock, and left to warm in candlelight.

tbilisi3.description: The page reads like a supra table photographed at dusk and bound into an ethnographic folio. The ground is a warm undyed-wool parchment (#F3E7D3) — the color of unbleached linen and shoti crust — carrying a barely-there tooth of paper grain so nothing floats on plastic white. Text sits in near-black walnut ink (#2A1D16), the tone of aged manuscript iron-gall on vellum. The brand's two anchors are a deep Kakheti saperavi wine (#5C1523) and a dark Caucasus forest green (#2E4232), used as full-bleed bands, rule lines, and inked panels rather than tints; where they meet, a hairline of hammered copper (#B87333) — reserved strictly for buttons, links, hover states and the reservation CTA — plays the wax-seal role, never a decorative fill and never body text. Ornament comes from the loom, not from clip art: a narrow repeating band of Georgian carpet geometry (zigzag chevrons, stepped diamonds, tiny hooked crosses) rendered as a 24px-tall wine-on-parchment strip separates major sections, and section numbers sit inside a small wax-seal roundel — a soft circular stamp of saperavi with a hand-cut edge. Typography sets manuscript against speech: headings in Cormorant Garamond at 600 and 700, wide-set with generous letterspacing on small caps eyebrows, its high-contrast strokes and calligraphic terminals echoing Mkhedruli-adjacent scribal weight; body in Alegreya at 400, 500 and 700 with its true italic for dish transliterations (khachapuri adjaruli, chakapuli, badrijani nigvzit), a text face with a warm, slightly rustic humanist rhythm that reads long and easy on parchment. Spatial rhythm is unhurried and archival: wide 96–128px vertical gutters between bands, a single 8-column measure for prose capped near 62 characters, and dish entries laid out like a catalogued collection — plate photograph above, Georgian name in small caps, English gloss in italic, a hairline copper rule beneath. Imagery is staged still-life in the ethnographic-archive manner: clay ketsi pans, hammered copper, walnut boards, blue-and-white ceramic, whole pomegranates, marigold and blue fenugreek in small dishes, arranged flat or three-quarter on dark wood, every object deliberately placed and held perfectly still. Texture is everywhere and quiet — paper grain on the base, a faint woven-cloth overlay behind the darkest bands, deckled edges implied by hairline rules rather than shadows. The mood is candlelit hospitality with the discipline of a museum vitrine: warm, sturdy, unhurried, entirely free of gloss.

tbilisi4.description: The page is set on a warm, undyed linen ground — #EFE3CF, the color of raw Georgian tablecloth cotton after decades of wine suppers, not a paper white and not a beige neutral. Across it runs a quiet lattice of hand-drawn ornament borrowed from Kakhetian textile borders and the carved wooden balconies of Old Town: thin zigzag chains, grape-leaf tendrils, and small eight-point rosettes drawn at hairline weight in a soft clay wash, used sparingly as band separators, list bullets, and a repeating border strip above the practical-information band — never as wallpaper. Body copy sits in deep walnut-bark #2E241C, dark enough to read like ink brushed on cloth. The primary voice is a fired brick-clay red #A8462C, taken from qvevri-earth and churchkhela dye — it carries headings, the ornamental rules, and the section eyebrows. A muted vineyard olive #565A34, the green of grape leaves and tarragon, supports as a secondary: it fills quiet tinted bands, tags dish categories, and underlines links. The accent, a burnished saffron-brass #7A5010, appears only on the reservation button and interactive states — a small struck-metal glint against all that cloth, never used for text blocks or decoration. Typography is entirely humanist. Headings are set in Alegreya at 700 and 500 — a calligraphic humanist serif with a genuinely Mediterranean, hand-cut warmth in its asymmetric serifs and slightly restless rhythm, which suits Georgian mkhedruli's own written quality far better than a rationalist display face; large sizes let its irregular stress read as brushwork. Body is Alegreya Sans at 400 and 600, with its true italic for dish descriptions and the story's quoted lines — a humanist sans whose open apertures and calligraphic terminals keep long paragraphs about supra and tamada feeling spoken rather than typeset. Numerals, prices, hours and the address line take Cormorant Infant at 500 — a delicate humanist old-style with soft, almost hand-shaped terminals — set in small caps-like tracking for menu prices and opening times. Spatial rhythm is generous but not precious: wide outer margins, dish content packed close in a measured column so the menu reads as an abundant table, story and location bands breathing wider. Cards hold their photographs flush to the card edge with the ornament and text stacked below on the linen. Photography is treated as if seen through aged silk: warmth held, saturation pulled back, highlights softened so khinkali steam, clay pots, walnut sauces and stone courtyards all sit in the same dusk-lit register as the ground. Overall the mood is a long table at dusk in a stone courtyard — hospitable, worn, hand-made, entirely uninterested in polish.

tbilisi5.description: This is a Georgian tavern rendered as a museum wall label: ceremonial, exact, and quietly reverent rather than cozy. The whole page sits on a light sage ground (#DCE2D3) — the muted green of oxidized copper roofs above Old Town Tbilisi, of dried tarragon and unripe walnut, of the pale wash behind a fresco after nine centuries of candle smoke. Body and headline text land on it in deep ecclesiastical charcoal-green ink (#1B2118), close to black but never neutral, so long paragraphs read like printed catalogue text rather than screen copy. The brand color is a deep pomegranate-oxide red (#8C2B22) taken straight from the ochre-and-madder register of Georgian cloisonné enamel and Svaneti icon panels; it fills solid graphic blocks, sets rules, and inks the ornament. A dull ceremonial brass (#6E5320) is the supporting note — hairlines, small caps labels, the thin frames around ornament badges, the glint of a chased silver-gilt vessel. A single saturated cobalt-teal (#1F5E63), the blue of enamel champlevé fields, is reserved exclusively for buttons, links and hover states so interaction never blends into the decoration. Typography speaks in one condensed voice with Swiss discipline: Oswald carries every heading in 400 and 600, set tight, uppercase for section titles with generous letter-spacing on the small ones, sentence case and near-zero tracking on the large ones — vertical, narrow, faintly monumental, like carved Georgian asomtavruli capitals translated into grotesque geometry. Body copy is Barlow Semi Condensed 400 and 500 with true italics for dish transliterations, keeping the narrow column rhythm while staying humane at 17–18px; numerals, prices, opening hours and address blocks step into Saira Condensed 500/700 uppercase for a tabular, timetable exactness. Ornament is structural, never sprinkled: flat vector blocks of Georgian borjgali rosettes, grapevine-and-cross interlace and manuscript marginal knotwork, drawn as solid pomegranate-red silhouettes inside precise square or half-square fields, deployed as full-width dividers between bands, as badges beside dish names, and as a repeating 8px-grid frieze at section thresholds — always aligned to the layout grid, never rotated or faded. Space is measured and generous but not luxurious: a strict 12-column grid, wide outer margins, section breaks marked by a 2px pomegranate rule above a stacked pair of condensed labels, and captions set in brass small caps at 11px. The mood is a curated exhibition of hospitality — the ceremonial table as artifact, laid out with the restraint of a Swiss poster and the gravity of an icon screen. Cards drop their boxes entirely: photograph above, condensed name, one line of ingredient text, a brass hairline beneath. Everything is square-cornered, printed, deliberate.

tbilisi6.description: This page is built to be read the way a tavern is entered — at dusk, on a phone in a narrow Sololaki lane or on a laptop in a hotel room after dark, by a traveller deciding where to eat tonight. So the ground is not paper but wall: a deep, warm-tinted stone brown (#231A14) that carries the whole page, the color of soot-darkened tuff and old cellar plaster, never black and never neutral. Body copy sits on it in a soft chalk-limewash (#EBDCC4) with generous line height so it reads like text brushed onto a wall rather than printed on a screen. Two Caucasus earth tones do the structural work: a deep fired-clay red (#8C3A24), the color of a qvevri's rim and of kilim wool, used for section grounds, rules, and heavy display fills; and an oxidized bronze-olive (#A8A277), pulled from copper cookware verdigris and dried tarragon, for secondary panels, dividers, borders and quiet labels. Reserved strictly for interaction — buttons, links on hover, the reservation call — is a candle-flame amber (#D9A441), which appears in small quantities and always reads as light rather than pigment. Nothing else is added; there is no fourth hue, no gradient, no glow. Typography is slab throughout, chosen for its blunt, carved, wood-and-iron character rather than any editorial refinement: headings in Zilla Slab at 600 and 700, its faintly angular slabs and slightly condensed rhythm recalling hand-painted Georgian shop signage where Mkhedruli and Latin sit side by side; body in Bitter at 400 and 600, a warm, sturdy slab with an open aperture that stays legible at small sizes on a dim screen, with its true italic used for dish transliterations (khachapuri, chakapuli, pkhali) and for the occasional Georgian toast pulled out as a line of pull-quote. A third voice, Cutive Mono at 400, sets menu category labels, hours, phone numbers and address lines in tracked uppercase — a typewriter register that suggests a hand-typed menu card slipped under glass, and keeps numerals unambiguous. Spatial rhythm is close and hospitable rather than luxurious: text columns held to roughly 62 characters, section padding measured rather than cavernous, menu items stacked in two dense columns on desktop with a bronze-olive hairline between each dish so the block reads as a written list, not a grid of tiles. Menu categories are separated by a full-width clay band, so scrolling through the food feels like moving from room to room. Corners are subtly softened everywhere — a small consistent radius on contained images and buttons — because this is a world of turned wood, clay vessels, and worn stone edges, with nothing machined or square about it. A faint concrete tooth lies across the whole page at very low opacity, giving the dark ground the grain of plaster under candlelight without ever muddying the type. Ornament is restrained and earned: thin double rules in bronze-olive above section titles, and small caps chapter labels — no borrowed pattern tiles, no ornate flourishes. Motion is slow and warm: sections settle upward into place as you scroll, images breathe almost imperceptibly, and hover states warm from chalk to amber like a wick catching. The overall feeling is of a low-ceilinged stone room where the only light is a hanging bulb and a table of candles, the food arriving out of the shadow.
